utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, The Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Very well. Today is the 22nd of January, 2008. My greetings to Ms. Dahl, to Mr. Seselj, to the witness and to all the people helping us. Before moving for a few moments to private session, let me say this: Today we are in Courtroom II, a rather small courtroom where you can't have many people in the public gallery since all the other courtrooms are taken up by trials with multiple accused. There is indeed a trial that is finishing. Therefore, we were given this courtroom, Courtroom II, and I believe we're going to stay here tomorrow as well because of the other hearings. This being said, since we are in Courtroom II there is a problem for Mr. Seselj's fax machine because he is an expecting a fax and the machine had been set up for the purposes of Courtroom I. As for Courtroom II, they're drilling through walls, installing cables, but it is not going to be ready before Thursday. So I don't know, Mr. Seselj. Are you going to be sent any faxes today? If so, we'll have to find a solution. Either we'll have to go and get them or you yourself will have to get them yourself. I have no ready-made answer. I know you wanted to say something about this. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, I avail myself of this opportunity since your advisor from the registry has already established contact with my legal advisor and he refused to send any documents by fax without my consent. To the fax of the registry, that is. On this occasion, I address my legal advisors telling them to send these documents that were supposed to send to me straight away to the registry fax. They're going to see this on the Internet now and I assume that by the next break they will have sent these documents. Could you please instruct the Mr. Doraiswamy to receive this on my behalf. I think that that is the easiest way of resolving the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, the legal advisors of Mr. Seselj are going to sent documents and they'll have to be picked up and handed over to Mr. Seselj. Good. This is going to be easy to solve. Let's move to private session for a few moments, please, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stoparic. Did you participate in military operations in Nevesinje in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called this Nevesinje, not in the town of Nevesinje itself but in the surrounding area, below Mount Velez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you asked to gather volunteers to participate in military operations there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. In order to clarify the matter for you, when I took part in the operations in the area of Mount Velez, Podvelezje, I spent a day in Nevesinje in order to get there. My base was at Grab, as it is called. It is a bit above Trebinje, and that is where we were asked to go out and help in the operations that were away, out of Grab. We -- in Grab we were under the command jurisdiction of another brigade but we were sent to help out another brigade. I think it was the Nevesinje Brigade. If that's what you meant by whether we were asked to come in and help as volunteers, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: In your unit, were there volunteers organised by the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander was Vojvoda Vakic, from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you estimate approximately how many Radical Party volunteers were under the command of Mr. Vakic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number varied. Some people went home and then new people would be brought in, but I don't know exactly. I think it was more than 100, but I cannot say. Please don't take my word for it. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you tell me what other units were present in that area that were organised by the Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that area, we were the only one, as far as I know. Somewhere else there was another unit too, but it was somewhere else. We did not have contact with them. I think Ljuba Ivanovic commanded that unit. I'm not absolutely sure of this. My understanding was while we were there that we were quite sufficient in that area. There were units in Trebinje itself, units of the Serb volunteer guard, or whatever they were called, organised by the SPO. And, of course the regular army, yes. Now, whether there was some other volunteer units there, probably, but I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: During this period, can you tell me whether Muslims were expelled from the area or the villages around Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were leaving. They were leaving, at any rate. There were individual cases of repression or whatever we call it. I think I've already told you that over there, I never experienced everything in an organised fashion, namely that somebody would issue a command saying go to a particular village and expel the Muslim population, but they were in jeopardy due to the fact that they did not have communications with the BiH army. One or two or three villages were within the Serbian enclave. I personally was in a few of these villages, in passing, in a car.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know whether volunteers under the command of Vakic participated in expulsions of Muslims from these villages?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some went, but as I already said, on their on bat.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe for me how the expulsions took place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not a direct participant in such events. But what I saw and what was a logical conclusion on my part was, was that two or three men would simply get into a car, go to a village, stop by a house, they would be offered coffee. Even if they wouldn't do a thing, that itself would intimidate the Muslims. Over there you could usually see only women and children and some elderly people. The younger ones, in my opinion, were either hiding somewhere in the woods in the area or in a way they had joined the BH army in some way and were active in its activities somehow. I don't know though. Once, I even saw one or two houses on fire there. My assumption is that one of us, the Serbs, had set the houses on fire, but I cannot really point a finger at anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were women or elderly persons cursed or beaten?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that I personally did not take part in any such thing, but quite frankly, had I participated in something like that myself, perhaps I would have resorted to. Well, I don't know. By the very fact that territorially, they were not linked up with the territories that were under the control of the Muslim army, the BH army, they were already frightened enough. I allow for that possibility, that perhaps there was some physical mistreatment too.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you saying with your testimony that the civilians were so frightened that they would flee simply upon the arrival of Serb forces such as the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, they cannot know at every point in time who is a volunteer and who is a member of the army of Republika Srpska or the army of Republika Srpska or anything. So many were members of the army of Republika Srpska and they wore a kokarda, if that is a Chetnik symbol, or I don't know. There would be some other small element that would be reminiscent of volunteers. However, the local people could make a distinction between volunteers and local members of the army by their accents. It's the same language, but we who come from Serbia have a different accent. They can recognise whether they were born there or whether we had come from Serbia. I am sorry. I have already forgotten by now. Now, what was your question; were they frightened when they would come in. It doesn't matter what kind of army goes through the village. I went through a few Muslim villages several times, or a few hamlets, rather. It was visible. Men would usually be running from the yards and hiding somewhere behind the walls. However, we would see that, we would registry that and nothing. We'd just go by. No one opened fire. Although I believe that sometimes some people did open fire at these patrols with hunting guns or something like that. However, I personally did not experience any such thing, so I cannot tell you about it in any greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Can you describe the activities of Captain Jovanovic's volunteer unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Captain Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Do you know what his unit was doing in the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I don't know Captain Jovanovic. Oh, you mean Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the same terrain, I was with him in the same unit once but that's not the area where I was together with him. Now we're talking about Podvelezje, Nevesinje. I don't know what his activities were. Like ours, I assume, protecting the positions. Now what they did when there was no active combat, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm asking you if you know what they were doing during the active combat.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same thing we were doing, taking part in combat. I'm not quite sure that I have understood you right, I mean, your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were you aware of local people who joined the unit in which you were participating in?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was customary. When we would come to a particular terrain, we would be joined by the local people. Not that many of them because, after all, they had military service there with the local army, the army of Republika Srpska. But a certain number would always join us. We needed them in a way, because, after all, these are people who are familiar with the area. We had just come there. We were not familiar with the area. So this had a practical purpose, too, the fact that we would take in a few people precisely from that area.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). As a matter of fact, I noticed, now, what should I call them? His countrymen in a way. I mean the people from that area stood in awe of him in a way. He is a big man. I think that he had his own truck before the war and I think that he was a driver who had his private business. So he is this big man. People out there were saying -- I can't remember what it was that he himself said, but there was a certain dose of respect vis-a-vis him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you ever brag to you that he had committed crimes against civilians in the area of Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for bragging, that's what fighters are prone to do. I mean, they brag a lot. Because in that way, they think that they are scoring points in a particular unit or in the general setting that they were in. During the war that was quite popular. I cannot remember exactly now. I know that he was saying something, but I cannot recall this very instant. I cannot remember a particular detail right now. It is very hard to remember all of these things too. Well, what he said, he did say. At any rate I'm going to convey this to you as, well, yes, there was knowledge to the effect that he had done something there, and it is not only that I had this knowledge but the local people had this knowledge too. As a matter of fact, people did know ...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of any SRS volunteers punished for mistreatment against civilians in this area?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, this is an incorrect question. The question wasn't asked first whether a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party had committed any war crime, first of all, so the Prosecutor can't imply that some crimes actually occurred and were perpetrated by the volunteers and then ask whether they were punished. Let's hear from the witness whether the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party to the best of his knowledge had committed any crime in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, you just skipped one step before putting that question. Before that, you have to identify the authors crimes, the perpetrators, so you have to go step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, are you aware of any SRS volunteers who committed crimes against civilians in the area of Nevesinje?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Dahl, you're asking me in open session to name names. I have already done that when we spoke about Vukovar for people that I had heard about or learnt that they had done something. And we were just speaking about a man, a particular man and how I know whether he did something or not. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, let's go into private session so that Mr. Stoparic can identify names that he does not wish to mention in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me -- thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me ask Mr. Stoparic to look at exhibit number 1885; that's the 65 ter number. It's at tab 40 of the Court binders. Mr. Stoparic, would you prefer a paper copy?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask the registrar to give the witness a paper copy. I'm handing 65 ter exhibit 1885 to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl, to save time and help us not to have to read the whole document, could you please summarize this document, saying, in this report coming from the command brigade -- coming from Commander Gusic in date of August 3rd, 1993. This is what has been said. And then will you ask the question. This is the technique that is traditionally used, and this morning, while reading the -- Mr. Seselj's examination by Mr. Milosevic, Judge Robinson thought that this was a bit lengthy and asked the parties to proceed is such a manner. So just sum up quickly the document and ask the position of the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this appears to be a report by Colonel Gusic, commander of the Nevesinje Brigade, signed also by a Captain Milenko, also known as Uco, commander of Dragi Lazarevic [phoen] regarding the report of soldiers of this unit killed or wounded in Podvelezje. It's a report directed to the Serbian Chetnik Movement, Serbian volunteer detachment, Belgrade. It is dated 3 August 1993 from Nevesinje and reports on members of the detachment from Trebinje in June 1992, specifically June 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, can you confirm whether this appears to be as described?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you show me this document that was the first time that I saw it. But I have no reason to doubt that this is an original document. It is quite customary, in other words, for reports to be sent on casualties in the way in which people got killed and according to our law, our combatants, when they seek their disability pensions in Serbia, they need to have a description of the event to base their applications on. What they also require is a stamp of the military post office, of the military garrison which is involved. It cannot be the stamp of the Radical Party. It has to be the military garrison's stamp to validate the application, and this is the way it was done in this particular report, mentioning the families of the killed, and my name is also indicated in this report in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask that the document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P28.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And if I can turn to exhibit 2118 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: -- which is at tab number 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Dahl. What did you want to say about this document, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the accused, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document is from a time when Mr. Stoparic had no longer been in Herzegovina, was no longer in Herzegovina. According to his statement at the beginning of the examination-in-chief at that time he should have been in the area of Brcko. We are talking about the 3rd of September, 1993. At that time, Mr. Stoparic was not there, not at that place. He was there in 1992, as we heard from his statement and this is over a year later. So that this is a report which was obviously made in order to regulate the combatants' status questions. This is it not a document from the time about which Mr. Stoparic is giving his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you yourself conducted investigation committee, so you are an expert when it comes to documents. If you read this one properly, which I doubt somehow, you would have realised that the name of the witness is to be found in this document. He is indicated as being having been wounded and hospitalised, and this won't have escaped you. The witness said here that at some point he was wounded, injured, so there is a direct link between the document and this witness who was injured. The very title of this document is report on soldiers of this unit killed or wounded in Podvelezje. So let's not waste time, Mr. Seselj. Please proceed, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, the next document is 65 ter Exhibit 2118. It's the addendum or addition to the report, and if I may have the paper copy tendered to the witness. You will find it at binder tab 42 and I will summarize briefly. It is, again, a -- marked as an addition to the report compiled by the author of the document we just discussed submitted to the Serbia Chetnik Movement, Serbian Volunteer Detachment, it is dated Nevesinje, 19 May 1995 entitled addition to the report on the troops from this detachment killed and wounded in Podvelezje. It describes combat activities on 26 June 1992, discusses who was wounded, including Mr. Stoparic, and it is signed by commander Lieutenant-Colonel Zoran Perkovic. The document is dated 1995. I'd request that it be marked for identification and I would ask Mr. Stoparic if the document appears to be as I've described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand the question? Have you seen this document, Mr. Stoparic? We can see your name in it, under number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is precisely that. In addition to the report, and that is what it says, on combatants killed and wounded. I am there in the first place. I don't know why, perhaps because I was deputy commander. Although, Your Honours, there is a mistake in respect of my birth date, 17th of January, 1958. It should be 17th of January, 1960, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This is noted. Mr. Registrar, a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, MFI P29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic --

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Actually, I said 1968, 17th -- the 17th of January, 1968. Everything else is correct here except the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document described your situation as a wounded soldier. Why was it sent to a political party? I'm trying to understand. Do you have an explanation for that or not? Indeed, if you were wounded, you were entitled to a military disability pension, unless the political party would also give you financial support. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether the political party gave any financial assistance. They probably endeavoured to assist the families of any killed or wounded combatants in the sense of providing information as to what they should do. Possibly also in financial terms. But it is quite possible that they have precisely such data in their archives which they can gain access to and use whenever they are necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I also notice, because, you know, nothing escapes me, I also noticed in this document that this document was also addressed to the 8th Motorised Brigade, apparently, of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It seems to be the brigade that was literally in charge of the unit that you were in. Is that so? Is this an accurate description of the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Let me next play a video-clip. It's 65 ter number 6066. And it is an interview of Mr. Seselj conducted by Laura Silber in March 1995 in which he is reflecting on activities during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, what I'm going to ask you to do is please listen to what Mr. Seselj says and then tell me whether or not your understanding of the operations he describes is consistent with what Mr. Seselj says.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: This is clip B, and it will be a compilation of several clips that I will play in succession and ask Mr. Stoparic to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpreters working from Serbian and working into English or French, could they translate so that we can check the translation that we see on the bottom part. In the future, whenever we have a video clip with Mr. Seselj or anybody else speaking Serbian, I'm requesting, demanding from the interpreters that they translate and not just to make do with what can be found on that strip in English, because sometimes that can cause problems. We're going to start again, and I'm demanding from the interpreters that they interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Interpretation. It is even too fast to read out the subtitles, let alone interpret it into French. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking the interpreters to listen to what Mr. Seselj says and to give a live interpretation. The interpreters are telling me that it is too fast, but we're going to try, all the same. Let's start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] In 1990, we were not acquiring weapons, we were only enlisting volunteers and occasionally when necessary from time to time we would send them to the front but those were very small groups. In 1991 we began organizing volunteers on a larger scale and sending them to already established front lines, particularly to eastern Slavonia here in the east of the Republic of Serbia Krajina. Our volunteers gave a very good account of this, especially in the battle in Borovo Selo which took place on the 2nd of May 1991 when they defeated stronger Croatian forces, Croatian police and para police forces. We were getting weapons from Milosevic's police from the then -- first from the then minister of internal affairs Radmilo Bogdanovic and when he was replaced from his successor. We were also getting all the weapons from the warehouse of the Territorial Defence. They were old American Thompson guns which had been withdrawn from use long time ago. There were also M48 guns, the so-called Tandzare guns. Therefore it was pretty much everything out of date that the army had already stopped using a long time ago and was kept somewhere in the warehouses of the Territorial Defence. They felt sorry to destroy all, so they just gave them to us, but it was with those weapons that we" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter could not catch the end of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl, your question, please. I remind you that you have already used five hours and 20 minutes, so you are 20 minutes beyond the time you were given initially. You have to complete this, because if we are too generous, we may run into problems. So please complete your examination-in-chief. But put your last questions first.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, with regard to the weapons, the source of weapons in cooperation with Mr. Milosevic identified by Mr. Seselj, is that congruent with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason whatsoever to doubt this, what Mr. Seselj says. I think that he is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we've just heard Mr. Seselj, who said this, I'll be very slow because every word he says in this interview may prove relevant later on. In the beginning, in early 1990s they dispatched some volunteers and then in 1991 there was a larger number of volunteers who were sent. That's what he said. But that's not my question. However, he addresses another problem, which is the arming of the volunteers and this is what he said. He said the volunteers received weapons from Milosevic's police. He gives the name of minister Bogdanovic and describes the quality, the poor quality of weapons. They're obsolete Thompson, M48, they're really obsolete. My question upon listening to him in the interview is whether the weapons given to the volunteers were given to them just before the volunteers were taken over by the JNA, because I believed that all of the volunteers were gathered in this, and this is from memory, in Potok, in a location called Potok and when the volunteers were gathered, were they given their weapons by the Radical party, to go then to the collection point, to be sent to the units, or did the volunteers go to a collection point and they were later given their weapons, issued their weapons. Can you tell us more about it? So I mention all the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge, which is not a lot, I don't know much about 1990, but what Mr. Seselj is saying about the outdated weapons and the various Thompson and outdated Tandzare guns, this is absolutely true. It is true that in the beginning we were supplied in this way. That is just my opinion and I cannot give you any proof. It was initially organised by the police, that is the information which I have, part of those weapons actually ended up in the arms of the Serbs who lived in Croatia. Initially it was distributed, it was precisely this weaponry that was distributed to the party members of the SDS. This is the way in which it was done and I have no reason to doubt that this is the way in which it took place at that point in time, as Mr. Seselj said. Later, when the army got more modern weaponry, this was organised in another fashion. It was by the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, the Yugoslav Peoples' Army provided every individual with better resources.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... The floor but let's be on the same wavelength and make sure we understand each other. You just said that the police would issue weapons. Now listening to you, I started imagining the fact that the police would issue weapons to citizens who were either reservists or would later become volunteers. These people, these individuals would then later go to collection points to be then assigned to JNA units. That's one possibility. There is another one. When there were volunteers, and said to the political party they were members of what their intentions were, did that political party that had received weapons from the police, did that body issue weapons to the volunteers. Third possibility, you have volunteers who leave their homes without any weapons, did they go to collection points where weapons were brought to them by members of the political party or by the JNA or other individuals. So as far as you know, which would be the case that would apply here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have very scant knowledge about that, precisely owing to the fact that as long as the police was involved, especially in the early periods of 1991, that was top secret to us. We had no way of knowing whom they were arming and why they were arming them. It is a fact that the weapons came from the police depot and many times the army actually denied that they had such weapons in their warehouses. Everything was conducted under a top secret regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Able to answer, but let's take your personal situation. When you became a volunteer, when were you issued a weapon and who was it issued by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got weapons in the temporary barracks that had been set up in Sid at the time. I joined as a volunteer member of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia Baranja and Western Srem and I was given the weapon by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you were concerned, you are telling us that you were issued a weapon by the JNA in this temporary barracks, and what kind of weapon was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember exactly, lorry drove up to the barracks. We were lined up outside the barracks. We had already set up a number of platoons and squads and we all knew that we would be attacking the village of Tovarnik. That's when the lorry drove up and the officers or the non-commissioned officers of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army opened up crates with weapons. We cleaned it, we degreased the weaponry and checked it for good order and that was all. Probably some records were also kept or some minutes were kept on that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What weapon did you get, an M48, a Kalashnikov or a Thompson, what did you get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was given an M70 gun, rifle, which you call a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you want to -- what did you want to say exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going to insist on this adamantly, but I should like to draw your attention to the fact that the question of relevance arises here. The indictment in all practice is not all that precise because the alleged joint criminal enterprise started prior to the 1st of August, 1991 according to it, so that my participation according to it lasts until September 1993, whereas these are events which took place much earlier. When we talk about 1992 -- 1990, we were persecuted in Serbia because of sending volunteers and this is a time which deals with the period prior to the JNA's clashing with the Croatian paramilitary forces. This is as far as the indictment is concerned, but I don't insist very much on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj pointed out that 1990 is outside the time-frame of the indictment and he fails to see any relevance to this topic. But maybe we can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is another video-clip regarding Mr. Seselj's assertions about the source of his weapons. So let's play clip E, which is the next clip in 65 ter number 6666, which is a composite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again I'm telling the interpreters to do what they did, is to interpret what can they can hear. "THE INTERPRETER: [Voiceover] That was all with Milosevic's knowledge, there is no doubt there, and a few from the police at the time with whom we established cooperation, were Radmilo Bogdanovic, Mihalj Kertes, and others. Franko Simatovic called Frenki and so on, who was the commander of the Red Berets later and so on. Then from the General Staff we mostly worked with General Domazetovic, who was at the time the deputy chief of the General Staff and the head of the personnel administration, if I remember correctly, but we also had contacts with lower ranking officers and so on. It all depended on the need and the situation. Our volunteers would come to Belgrade to the Bubanj Potok barracks, and there they would put on uniforms, they would be issued with weapons and busses and from there they would go to where they were needed. And they were under the command of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army as soon as Yugoslav Peoples' Army got involved in the conflicts."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the transcript, we could not hear the journalist's question very well. But we were able to here Mr. Seselj's answer perfectly. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Were there members of the Radical party staff present at the distribution of weapons at Bubanj Potok?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember once in the Bubanj Potok barracks we were visited by Zoran Drazilovic. He even issued with kokades there, but whether he was literally there where the weaponry was being distributed, that I cannot claim with certainty. I don't know why he would have been there. That is the obligation of some of the officers who were present there but he did come to visit us and he would stay there for a while. I was there twice. I was there for one week for a short training course and then we were sent to the field from there to the airport and then to the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Ljubisa Petkovic ever present when weapons were being distributed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not any weapons were stored by Radical Party members in Sid to be distributed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether members of the Radical Party kept it in Sid. What I do know is that at a certain point in time a small amount of weaponry was kept in the garage of Milenko Petrovic but it was forwarded on. But it was not organised by the Radical Party. It was organised by the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you mentioned a small detail that may not be that relevant but is relevant to me. You said that you were given a kokade. I suppose that's the kokade representing the political party; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We already referred to kokades. A kokade is a symbol hailing from the Second World War, generally a symbol of the Serbian army which is worn on the cap. There are different variants and there are different designers of the kokade. We were all issued with one at the time by Zoran Drazilovic. That was in the Bubanj Potok barracks, and I remember well that he said, lads, don't put it on now. After you leave you can put it on your caps and your heads but as long as we're here we have to respect our host and we have to wear his emblems and not any different ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the official emblem of the JNA, wasn't it this five-point star?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should have been, but very quickly, I believe at the very outset of the war this changed. This was for a very short period, but officially, yes, that was the emblem of the JNA, and when I served the regular army, it was the five-pointed star.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you became a volunteer and joined this volunteers unit, did you have this kokade, kokarde and a five-point star or only this kokarde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We got weapons and equipment from them, all the necessary equipment from uniforms to everything else. But we did not get any emblems from them. Sometimes they would be already sewn on the uniforms, the patches would be already sewn on to the uniforms, but not on our caps. The caps had a five-pointed star already as a component part of the cap. So we were issued the five-pointed stars when we were given these caps in that sense, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You received that kit, the equipment, pants, socks, weapons. Did you -- did you have a helmet and did you have this five-point star engraved, embossed in the helmet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It may now be time to have a break. Ms. Dahl, normally the examination-in-chief is over. Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question. I had one or two follow-up questions of Mr. Stoparic and would like to have the videos marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, one moment. Yes, we'll come back to this. First numbers for the video-clips, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Ms. Dahl, I'm going to try and be as clear as possible, because sometimes I thought you did not understand me. It may be my fault. I'm taking on the responsibility for it. So back to the topic. The Trial Chamber decided to give you five hours for the examination-in-chief. Presently we've nearly reached five hours and 30 minutes, so you're 30 minutes beyond the initial time allotted to you, which is not admissible [as interpreted], because otherwise, the balance would not be respected in the proceedings. So I repeat, when a party is given a finite amount of time by the Trial Chamber, the party has to comply with the time restraint. It is ruled out that they get additional time, because this may carry certain consequences. It so happens that you're already 30 minutes beyond your time. So you have to put an end to your examination-in-chief. You said that you had one or two follow-up questions. Fine. Okay. But after those two, are you done?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I will conclude my examination in accordance with the Chamber's instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if we have a few minutes left, put these one or two follow-up questions and then your examination-in-chief will be completed. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I want to turn your attention, Mr. Stoparic, to preparations for going into action at Bosanski Grahovo and Livno. With regard to a kokarde, did you receive a similar instruction from Ratko Mladic about how to wear that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, in terms of similar use?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Well, General Mladic visited you then; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Kresits is the name of the place, and it was a factory for manufacturing some agricultural material, as far as I remember correctly. But as for the kokarde, he said that we should carry it in our hearts, not on our heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did he give you instructions about how to treat civilians when taking Livno?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he said that up to Livno, he is not even interested in pets. That's what he said, ironically, and in Livno he said that we should take care of civilians. Not more, not less. Literally that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean when he said that on the way to Livno he was not even interested in pets?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How did I understand this... That he wasn't interested in the prisoners probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Did you understand that they could be killed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was the ethnic makeup of Livno?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that the vast majority of the population is Croat but I'm not sure. Before the war I had never been to Livno, never in my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: And what was your understanding of the meaning of Mladic's instructions to take care of the civilians in Livno?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't even try to understand him. For me, he was a legend. What he said, that is the way I thought things should be. It wasn't only me. It was everybody. He said that in Livno we should take care of civilians. Probably not to be cruel towards civilians. At any rate, to take care of civilians. We all know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: What was your understanding of what he said regarding caring your hat in your heart instead on your head?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's not the only one who used to say that. Many JNA officers -- well, then he was not a JNA officer. Maybe he was. I can't remember exactly. But many of the officers, in view of the training and education they had, they did not give an oath to Serbian state but to Yugoslavia and many thought that the kokade was not needed, rather the five-pointed star and it was my understanding that what he meant, the fact that you like Serbia and are a Serb, you should bear that in your heart, it doesn't have to be on your head, that was my understanding of it. I'm going to give you this other observation that was there. There was also a technical problem on account of kokades. If a Croat would happen to see you through his sights and if he would see me with a kokade and another one with a five-pointed star, I think he's going to kill me first.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Was that because it represented you or identified you as a Chetnik?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Croats called all the Serbian soldiers Chetniks, but I would have been an ideal target for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: With that, Your Honour, I will conclude my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dahl. We will now break for 20 minutes. Could Mr. Registrar do what needs to be done to get the faxes that were sent by Mr. Seselj's associates and hand them over. I am being told that Mr. Seselj's has already received his faxes. That's one problem off the list. And we will meet -- we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Now before giving the floor to Mr. Seselj for the cross-examination, let me talk about the problem with the videos and their interpretation. I'm asking both parties, Prosecution as well Defence, the following: When they intend to show a video, they must hand it to the Interpretation Service before the hearing, this video, saying that they intend to play the video. Therefore, the interpreters can hear and see the video beforehand in order to be able to interpreted it in court. Secondly, we gave some MFI numbers to these videos. The Trial Chamber has noted the observations of Mr. Seselj and can only admit these videos when it will have the script in English of what was said in that video. This is the way we will proceed. These technical problems have been taken care of. I will now give the floor to Mr. Seselj for his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stoparic, we're going to start with some parts of your CV that I'm particularly interested in. From the documents we managed to find out some basic information about you up until 1990. Sometime in May 1990, you were wounded in a clash with Albanian terrorists in Kosovo and Metohija, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then you were treated at the military medical academy in Belgrade. Was that at the VMA or some other hospital?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The VMA inter alia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, it is too fast and there is overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot follow the questions and answers because of the overlap of the speakers, and I request that Mr. Seselj be reminded to slow down and an allow a pause for the interpretation of his question and likewise the interpretation of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. This is a well-known problem here in this Tribunal. When two people speak the same language you must absolutely give some time in order for the interpreters to be -- to have time to translate the question before the answer starts, and the same for -- otherwise the interpreters can't follow, and the Judges can't follow either. So Mr. Seselj and Mr. Stoparic, please make sure that you wait between the question and the answer. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: My direct question, Mr. Stoparic, after your medical treatment, you returned to Sid, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was in 1999?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, for about a year, I was still busy with medical treatment. I practically have to have this bandage on my hand for almost a year and every two months I went to the institute where employees of the MUP of Serbia are treated medically and then they would extend my sick-leave. As for my salary, I went directly to the SHA base in Batajnica myself in order to collect my salary and after that, I already became entitled to a disability pension. It wasn't too big but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So after completing your hospitalisation because you stayed there for a bit over a year, you were -- you had paid sick-leave as a member of the reserve force of the police?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And after that, when that was completed, you got the status of a war invalid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since when have you had this status, in tentative terms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I don't have it any longer. I don't know if now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a review and I was not in the country, and I received a decision stating that I had to be present for the review. That is the usual procedure. For a year, year and a half you are a war invalid, and that you go for a general review and then you get a permanent document, but I couldn't do it because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So sometime in 2000 you obtained the status of a war invalid?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly. While I was in the state of obtaining this status during the course of that year, I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... There's inadequate pause between the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, you're speaking much too fast, both of you. So please allow for a pause between the questions and the answers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'm going to exercise even stricter control over myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me, how big was this disability payment, roughly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am not going to speak in dinars because that changed, but I'm going to go speak in terms of Euros. Well, I don't know. About 50 Euro.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: One could hardly live on that, could one?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you do anything else in order to be able to survive?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, I had two brothers who helped me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They practically supported you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Practically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how long did that go on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know until when that went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, afterwards my hand got better so I would do something, if possible, but literally it went on until I left Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you what country you live in. I'm really not interested in that. But tell me, when did you leave Serbia, what year?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 2004.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So for all of four years, you lived on roughly 50 Euro a month and on the assistance you received from your two brothers. That was a very hard life, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you were there yourself at the time and you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, both people are speaking at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Life was like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From then onwards, you were in a western country. From 2004 onwards, did you ever return to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that for all of four years now you have been abroad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't want to disclose your place of residence in any way. I would just be interested in your way of life over these past four years. Namely, are you staying at a hotel?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you have an apartment of your own?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's still not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's paid by the Office of the Prosecutor of the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm not seeing the relevance of these questions. Perhaps the relevance was in the last question, but -- so I withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am questioning the credibility of this witness, Mr. President, and I did not put a single question that is not in keeping with procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objection had been withdrawn, so you can condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now what is it that I'm interested in now. Is it paid for by a foreign government, by The Hague Tribunal, or a third party. You don't even have to say who the third party is.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the third party. I'm paying for it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is your current revenue?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you exactly how much money I make every month, well, that's relative, because I have a company of my own and I never know how much money I'm going to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now you have a company of your own abroad?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It works well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I opened it only about a year ago, but I managed to repay my loans and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The question/answer is speeding up again and I'm seeing that they're overlapping the interpreters, and I would like to be able to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Mr. Seselj, please, take care of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, Your Honour. It's not Mr. Seselj's fault. I understand him before there is an interpretation, so I give fast answers. I'll do my best not to do that in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the previous three years before you opened this company, what is it that you lived on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while -- well, it is not a secret that I was in the relocation programme of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you lived on their donations, contributions, monthly contributions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can you remember how many money that was per month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is not against some rules here, I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, it is not against any rules.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would be 30 Euro per day, quite literally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is about 90 Euro a month, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 900 Euros a month, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For those three years?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I became independent earlier on. I opened a company a year ago, but before that, I took a job so I made my own money.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how long did this status of yours go on when you lived only on the assistance provided to you by The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say about two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Two years. And could one live normally on 900 Euro a month?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did. I tried. It wasn't really that much money in the west, but one could live a normal life. It's not that I did not have many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So now you're not enjoying the status of a witness that the Tribunal takes care of, that is to say, a witness that is supported by the Tribunal and giving him certain amounts of money or whatever?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You're a foreigner, although you're resident in a foreign country and nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were brought in for an interview by the OTP before this testimony. Is that right? That was on the 3rd of January, this year.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were asked here to the headquarters of the Tribunal and they started preparing you for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long did these preparations last?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, up until the testimony started itself, a day before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many days was that? Every day up until the testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many hours per day?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think for as long as the hearing takes place here, so it's not the entire day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: About four hours?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And during these preparations there was a problem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What problem do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were not prepared to confirm that at the first rally of the Serb Radical Party in Sid, I used the Hitler salute to greet the persons present there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that is what was in your statement that the OTP made you sign, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Seselj, I am sorry for addressing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're answering a question at every meeting and I cannot recall exactly what the question was and how come this comparison came up with Hitler, probably with the speed involved and everything. I would never say that a Serb resembled Hitler.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was said here specifically was that I used the Hitler salute to greet the persons present there.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I have two objections. First, Mr. Seselj is mischaracterizing what the statement says, and second, he interrupted the question and did not let him finish giving the explanation he was giving to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's go back to this Hitler salute, Hitler greeting. Could you say in which paragraph of the written statement this is mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to page 2 of the OTP document dated the 7th of January 2008, the third paragraph, where it says that I addressed the masses as Hitler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But this document comes from the proofing between Prosecution and the witness. And the witness must have changed either a word or a sentence that was in his 2006 statement. Maybe Ms. Dahl could tell us in which paragraph in the 2006 statement we can find this.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is at paragraph 55 which is on ERN number 06031470, and if you'd like I could find the e-court number if you'd like it displayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that this is not being taken from my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On paragraph 55, it says that Seselj addressed the crowd like Hitler. Please continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say that I really greeted the masses of people present as Hitler or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the preparations for this trial I noticed the same thing and I tried to give an explanation. During the proofing with the Prosecutor, never ever would I say that of a Serb, that he resembled Hitler in any way. It is only possible that there was this comparison made in the heat of the speech or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But, Mr. Stoparic, allegedly you signed this statement. Does that mean that you did not read it before having signed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read it but not as carefully as I did the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't read it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is very hard to go on for hours and you can barely wait to stop and go and take a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you were not focussed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were therefore other omissions in the same way in this statement, right? There were some things that you didn't want to have in your statement that found their way into the statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the first day of the examination-in-chief you stated here that you do not recall when the first rally of the Serb Radical Party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This problem of the Hitler salute, could the witness please look at paragraph 55 in his own language and could he please read out in his own language what is written.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm tendering the signed original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, could you look at paragraph 55. In the middle of this paragraph, after the word "radnike," there is the sentence that starts with "Seselj."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read it out loud in your own language and we will get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Seselj greeted the persons gathered there like Hitler and he was" -- Shall I go on? "Asking the Croats to leave Serbia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor, you stated that you did not remember when this rally of the Serb Radical Party in Sid took place exactly, right? You don't know whether it took place in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Now I really don't know when each rally took place because it wasn't that there was only one rally. There were several.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But the Prosecution made you sign this; namely, that this rally took place in the summer of 1991 and you did sign that. Because you were not focussed enough; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that I have to say this every time that I wasn't focussed enough. Of course I tried to be focussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you omitted that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether it was an omission or an oversight. I don't know the exact date and perhaps I gave a tentative one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I will give you the exact date. The first rally in Sid was held on the 15th of May, 1992, during the election campaign for the federal elections. Have I jogged your memory now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You haven't, because I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. I'm stating that piece of information here now because it's contained in the archives of the Serb Radical Party and this can be checked with the authorities in Serbia because every rally has to be registered with the police. Every public gathering has to be registered with the police. This rally took place on the 15th of May 1992 according to the information of the Serb Radical Party the municipal committee in Sid was established on the 5th of November, 1991. That is to say, after you went into the war. Over here, the Prosecution insisted that you went into the war because you were inspired by the speech I made at the rally that was held a year later. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know when that rally was held. But I'm almost convinced that I had heard you before going into the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You could have heard me on television too, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was part of TV shows, radio shows like any other politician?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible, that's quite possible. Because were quite popular.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you took part in the war on several occasions. Did you personally -- are you personally proud of your participation in the war? You personally with your conduct, your behaviour and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was never sorry that I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were never sorry, right. Now from the Prosecution here you were given something to sign and they say that you made a -- a step which was a mad step to join up. Now, does that correspond to what you said or is this something that was put in by the Prosecution arbitrarily?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, could we have the paragraph number?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Paragraph 4. N06031337, in the same step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, this is the problem: When we read paragraph 55 at paragraph 4, we get the feeling that in Sid you heard Mr. Seselj's speech, the speech he gave on the football field; and that was in the summer 1991. And then on paragraph 4 we see that either in August or September, you go and volunteer. Mr. Seselj has just told us that this speech was held on May 15th, 1992, later on. So if you left in September 1991 to volunteer, then this has nothing to do with the speech. What's the real story? You see in your own language you signed a document saying that it was in September 1991 and there's a logic with paragraph 4. But if the speech was held on May 15th, 1992 for the regional elections, then this could -- this is a problem. A Judge would wonder about this, which is normal. So if as it says in paragraph 4, you know, you volunteered, we'd like to know whether you volunteered just out of your own accord or did you volunteer after having heard a speech?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said several times that by getting to know about Mr. Seselj and his concepts, some of his concepts, well, it's not essential for me whether I heard it a year later or not. He was making speeches even before that and I always said that he's not the only person that inspired me and that is only because of Mr. Seselj and his programme that I went to war. There's something that is called patriotism which prompted me and the fact that I believe many of the things that Mr. Seselj said, that's the truth of it, and what I said that it was as describing it as an insane step, I did say that, because well, not my decision to go to war. I'm proud of going to war, but it was an insane decision to go and be killed, to go and die.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since you are proud, Mr. Stoparic, of your participation in the war - and I congratulate you for that, very sincerely - did you consider during the fight for the liberation of Vukovar yourself to be a part of some monstrous plan, and after the fighting ceased, did you consider this in Vukovar to be part of a monstrous plan which I devised or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know whether anybody devised a monstrous plan. I personally did not feel to be a part of any monstrous plan, no, I personally did not feel myself to be part of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, as a man who was at one time a member of the Serbian Radical Party but no longer are, but as somebody who is proud of your wartime past and your past as a combatant, did you consider that I personally tricked you by any of my public appearances or by delivering any of my speeches?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was dis -- have been disillusioned with all the relevant politicians of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were probably disillusioned with respect to the consequences, the unsuccessful fighting, the routing that the Serbs experienced in Serbian Krajina and in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that too, and the loss of territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But do you consider that I lied to you and other people in striving for the defence of Serbian Krajina Republika Srpska and the defence of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consider to this day that had fate made you president, had that been the destiny, things might have looked very different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Stoparic, for that trust and confidence. So what your answer is is that you don't think that I lied to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you lied to us. You said what you felt and it's up to us -- it was up to us to believe you or not. I personally did believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the Prosecution slipped in something that they wanted you to sign and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That I became part of the monstrous plan of Slobodan Milosevic, and that is to be found in paragraph 6. It says: "Hence I cannot reproach myself that much, even now, for becoming part of Slobodan Milosevic's monstrous global plan."

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was speaking about you, not about Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does that mean that a monstrous plan on the part of Slobodan Milosevic did exist whose goal was to liberate Vukovar from the Croatian paramilitary forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I didn't. But I didn't use that word in association with Vukovar. Probably it referred to all my disillusionment and disappointment, but let me add something. There is some culprit, someone to blame, and as I feel that I have been let down, then it is Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down once again, thank you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that we were brave enough and had enough weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, where, then, lies the monstrosity of this alleged -- yes, yes, I will do my best. I get carried away, but I will nonetheless do my best again. Does that mean that some monstrous general plan, global plan existed on the part of Slobodan Milosevic whose component parts are both you and I, that we are component parts of that plan, or do you hold it against Milosevic for being at the head of Serbia during those years and the Serb people were unsuccessful in their fighting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I hold it against him. Not only was he not successful in his battle, but we all know what happened to the Serbian people. As to the monstrous plan, well, it would be a very bad thing if Milosevic as the president of state did not have a plan for all those many years. Now somebody -- some people refer to this plan as monstrous. I do not, Mr. Seselj. I have changed some of my visions and opinions, the ones that I held when I was 23 years old and I don't say that sometimes it is difficult for me to go back to say what I thought in 1991 and to distinguish between what I feel today. They are intermingled, but I'm sure you will understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a volunteer, you reported to the territorial defence of Slavonia Branja Western Srem directly, is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was by chance that I heard one day that they had offices in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At that time the Serb Radical Party did not have an office.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that same office, when the TO of Slavonia Branja and Western Srem left, then the offices became the offices of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that was because otherwise, this was a building where the political parties had their offices. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Socialist Party had its office there, too, and various other parties as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And now here from the Prosecution they slipped in a document for you to sign saying that this -- these representative offices of the Territorial Defence of SBWS existed in parallel. Or, rather, Eastern Slavonia and Western Srem and the seat of the Serbian Radical Party. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party at the time was already being established or perhaps it had already been informed, but that was in Mr. Milenko Petrovic's private house so perhaps this went on parallel to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
