utterances.text: Now, I am putting to you the following: That the Serbian Radical Party in Sid in the house belonging to Milenko Petrovic was established on the 5th of November, 1991, and furthermore, that it was only in March 1992 that it was given state offices by the Sid municipality in the building of the former committee where otherwise the other political parties were put up, this being vital movement and renewal movement and all the others?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what parties exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But am I right in what I'm saying in general terms?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the exact date when these offices were given over to political organisations, but that's not difficult to check out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Certainly. The municipality has it on their records when it gave out the offices to the different parties because it was a regular act in conformity with the laws. Every political party had the right to be given offices, premises if it had a Municipal Board in the municipality in question, isn't that right, and then this was reduced to parliamentary political parties because 300 parties registered and then it was only the parliamentary parties that were able to get state-owned premises. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was probably like that. And of course it depended on the respect that the political parties had at a local level. If it was a large party it didn't matter that in other towns they weren't as strong but if they happened to be strong locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So we've dealt with those questions and we will move on to another area, another set of questions. For a time you were in the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we move on to something else, this is a very important question, because there are two different situations. If, in September 1991, you volunteer in the premises of the TO without there being a -- an office of the Serbian Radical Party, then the conclusion that can be drawn is that at that time the Serbian Radical Party has nothing to do with the fact that you volunteered in September 1991, but maybe you went there in September 1991 to the TO's offices, to the office and there was an office of the political party and an office of the TO and then the situation is very different. Earlier Mr. Seselj told us that Petrovic set up the Serbian Radical Party on November 7, 1991, almost two months after you volunteered, and that his party had a premise in that very building in March 1992. So things here are very different and the consequences are very different. So to your recollection, could you tell us how things were exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I've always said that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I want things to be very accurate, because in my -- the way I look at criminal law, there's no approximation. Things are very specific and very accurate. We cannot have any margins for interpretation. This is very important. You volunteered, in brackets, to the TO in November 1991, and I want to be absolutely convinced beyond any reasonable doubt that the day you went to that office there was only the TO there and no other political party. The accused told us that the premises were given to his party in March 1992, six months later. So what exactly can you confirm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I started out as a volunteer of the Territorial Defence of Slavonia Branja Western Srem and I never mentioned that my first engagement was in the organisation of the Serbian Radical Party. Now, as far as the dates are concerned, I really don't know. I have no reason to doubt anyone not to believe them and without the offices, the Serbian Radical Party existed in my town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The Serbian Radical Party existed for almost four months before given premises. We have an official piece of information that it was established on the 5th November 1991 but that's after you went to war. Mr. Stoparic, I'm not interested in this first involvement of yours because you weren't a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party at the time nor did you have anything to do with the volunteers. However, you do mention something else, the training at Lipovaca, for instance. What has this Lipovaca got to do with the Serbian Radical Party or Serbian Chetnik Movement? Can it have any connections at all. Anything to do with them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the Serbian Radical Party has with the training camp. I have already said who conducted the professional training course. It's somebody who didn't look like a radical nor did he introduce himself as a radical. But from there, from that camp we were sent to Supoderica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Then it says in your statement something else, that you had some Chetnik instructors or rather instructors from the Chetnik Movement and they probably looked like Chetniks, but did you have any proof and evidence to show that from the Serbian Chetnik Movement they were within the Serbian Radical Movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not how they introduced themselves or presented themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That means that in paragraph 22, what it says there, that was something put in, slipped in by the Prosecution because it's something that they needed to do because what is mentioned here is the Serbian Chetnik Movement and of course when you the Serbian Chetnik Movement in this way, then this associates one with the Serbian Radical Party and its component parts, but that's what you actually meant to say. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that a number of people introduced themselves as being Chetniks, members of the Chetnik Movement if I can put that way. And, Mr. Seselj, we both know that it's not the Serbian Radical Party who's the only one that had a section of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Many people did and I met or, rather, I saw various ID booklets from Serbian Chetnik Movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you without giving a leading question and suggesting the answer. But, anyway, thank you. So when somebody's referred to as a Chetnik, that in principle means absolutely nothing with respect to belonging to the Serbian Radical Party, for instance, or its section of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually when you see a bus going past with volunteers and if it has a poster with your image on it, then that most probably is something organised by the Serbian Radical Party. But I have to be quite honest. There were various sections, so-called sections, but if somebody introduces himself as a Chetnik then I'm not anybody in authority to question them or ask for their IDs. I just take what he says at face value.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. So the Serbian Radical Party, with this training in Lipovaca, could not have had any links with that, anything to do with that. That's all I'm interested in. I don't want to go into the other details.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know for sure. All I do know is that I went from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you don't know that this was linked to the Serbian Radical Party. That's what I want to know. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that the guys who were there were from the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Some Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They didn't say which particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, I will slow down again. Now, later on, as a reservist of the First Guards Brigade, according to your statement, you were transferred to the Leva Supoderica Detachment, the Territorial Defence of Vukovar. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That entire group from that place that was called Lipovaca, we went there, except the people who they asked before sending them whether they were afraid and if they were afraid, they could step down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, in the Supoderica Detachment, you found the citizens, locals from Vukovar, you found the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and you also came across other volunteers who did not belong to the Serbian Radical Party. Is that the truth of it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were people --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That corresponds to what you said in your examination-in-chief, your testimony during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The accused interrupted the witness's answer. I'd like him to be able to finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please finish your answer, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the question was at this point. 200 questions have been addressed to me. You have to tell me which particular question you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was the question on page 63 [as interpreted], line 5. You said, yes, there were people and then there's some dots or question marks. Mr. Seselj, would you mind asking the question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope you won't take this away from my valuable time. My question was: Did Mr. Stoparic, in the Leva Supoderica Detachment, find people who were the local people of Vukovar, people who were volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, and people who were volunteers but not from the Serbian Radical Party and he gave me an answer in the affirmative. So I only noted that that corresponded to his statement which he gave during the examination-in-chief and that was all that was to it, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what is your answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that in the Leva Supoderica Detachment there were people who were locals, local people of Vukovar or from the surroundings and also there were people from the Serbian Radical Party who had arrived there in an organised fashion as well as other people who joined it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I'd like to go back to this topic addressed by Mr. Seselj, because I'm trying to see, to dissect everything you said and I want to avoid any confusion or misunderstanding. You spoke about the three instructors or the three people who instructed the volunteers. You give their names. I'm going to mention one of them. I'm sure that's going to help you remember, because you said Ljubo Ivanovic is the name. He was a Chetnik captain from Nis and you said that he was the one in charge, the boss. And I discover that this captain was later killed during the war. In paragraph 24, you explained that when he was killed there was his funeral in Nis and you said that Mr. Seselj sent a letter after he died. I'm trying to reconstruct all of this, because, you see, what I want to know is whether the investigators tried to get you to say certain things that you would later have signed without realising the import of what you have said. Do you remember this Captain Ivanovic? He was an instructor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have said that Captain, not Jovanovic, but Ivanovic was there, that he had introduced himself as the person who would be explaining some things that we needed when -- in fighting. I also said that another person going by the nickname of [indiscernible] did all the other instructing, and he seemed to me to be the more competent person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This captain, Captain Ivanovic was he, as far as you know, a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that particular moment, in September, October of 1991, I'm not quite sure, I don't know. I just know that there was this Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So why did you tell the investigators that when he died in combat, he -- Mr. Seselj sent him a letter? How do you know that? Why would Mr. Seselj have sent a letter because of the funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was at that funeral myself, and there were very many people attending the funeral after this man had been killed. This letter was sent by Mr. Seselj and it was publicly read out to all of us as a sign of gratitude for his contribution in the battles that had been conducted for the offence [as interpreted] of the Serbian lands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You attended the funeral, you were present when the letter was read out. We don't have the letter. Was it a letter that paid homage to a member of the Serbian Radical Party or was it to pay tribute to a captain who was killed in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You asked me, Honourable Judge, whether I knew that he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party in 1991. This funeral took place several years later, and I don't know about 1991, and I cannot say about 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, in order not to lose time, I can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ljuba Ivanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Seselj is interrupting the witness. I'd like him to be able to finish his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give Mr. Seselj the floor. But could you complete what you were saying, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply said in answering your question whether he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party in 1991, I don't know that. I know that he introduced himself as a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Later I came to know him better and I took part in some actions together with him. Then he was a member of the Serbian Radical Party and was killed in Herzegovina in combat as a member, but I don't know whether he was one in the first moments when I had met him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, we shall deal with that question when we deal with the question of Herzegovina. Indeed Ljuba Ivanovic joined the Serbian Radical Party in 1992 and went to Herzegovina as a volunteer but I leave that for when we deal with the question of Herzegovina. What is of the essence here is that if he was in Lipovaca at that time he could not have had any connections with the Serbian Radical Party. Because a political party is an organisation with a fluctuating membership. One can be a member one day and not the next. It is not something that is unchangeable and it is open to fluctuating, but we shall deal with that question when we come to the question of Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... These are submissions, not questions and I ask that we return to examining the witness rather than making submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, you should have told the witness, if I were to tell that you Mr. Ivanovic joined the Serbian Radical Party in 1992, would you agree with that or not? Then the witness could have said, I don't know, yes, you're right, et cetera. Let's move on. It is now in the transcript that in Mr. Seselj's view, Captain Ivanovic joined the Serbian Radical Party in 1992. That's it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain to the Bench why I'm leaving this for later. What is much more important for me is for us to deal with this question, and this is because my time is running out fast, is the question of Vukovar. The commander of that unit, of the Leva Supoderica unit was Milan Lancuzanin. Was he not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was a reserve captain first class, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps he had a higher rank. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is what I remember. Captain first class because reserve officers could go -- only be promoted up to that rank in the former Yugoslavia. He was already the commander of the TO when the Guards Brigade arrived there and when the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party came. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a local. He is a local. He had participated in some operations in the vicinity of Vukovar even before we arrived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. Let us dwell on this question of Chetniks in Vukovar some more. You know, Mr. Stoparic, from the time that the radical party -- Serbian Radical Party was set up on the 23rd of February, 1991, that no supreme organ of the Serbian Chetnik Movement ever convened or met? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. Shall I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that you tried to register a party with that name, under that name and later you registered the Serbian Radical Party. Now, whether any supreme or high organ existed and if was called that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory, Mr. Stoparic. We tried to register the Serbian Chetnik Movement in 1990 when the other political parties registered also. That was in August 1990 and the regime denied us to register on the 23rd -- on the 23rd of February, 1991, we had a congress of unity of unification in Kragujevac where the Serbian Chetnik Movement unified with most of the boards of the Serbian Radical Party and the Serbian Radical Party was established. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something of the kind transpired, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it is odd to my mind that you had never heard after the Serbian Radical Party had been set up in February 1991 that at the summit an organ, a special organ of the Serbian Chetnik Movement convened. You have not heard -- you had not heard.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, it is so because nothing of the kind existed. Had something of that kind existed, you would have heard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It would have been in the media, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As regards Chetnik emblems in Vukovar, you refer to kokades. Did the Serbian Radical Party ever produce any kokades or emblems of its own? Or are we referring to kokades that were manufactured by different manufacturers and were sold in the streets of Belgrade and other Serbian cities?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All these symbols, the kokades or even emblems with words or with the letters SCP, Chetnik Movement, could be bought around the railway stations questioning the streets and [indiscernible] in the streets, that is how I obtained my first kokade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know for a fact that the Serbian Radical Party or the section of the party, the Serbian Chetnik Movement, itself produced some of these or commissioned these with the manufacturers, some specific emblems?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember anything of the kind. May have happened, might have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But had it been the case, you would have known of it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only had occasion once to get a kokade from Zoran Drazilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually it was from Ljubisa Petkovic, not Zoran Drazilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It happened to me when I went to see the combatants at the front line to fill my pockets with kokades that I had bought from street vendors and then hand them out to the combatants who wanted to have them.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also done by Radovoj [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And many other people and this was because none of us could bear the sight of the five-pointed star as a communist symbol, is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We called ourselves reservists, Chetniks. The reserves called themselves Chetniks and the others were referred to as parties as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will parties please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the soldiers, when they got their caps they would actually tear off the five-pointed stars from their caps, off their caps. They didn't want to wear it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: May I remind both parties but particularly the witness to observe a pause. Maybe you should train yourself to count to five after Mr. Seselj has spoken before you speak yourself. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were different types of kokades. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Depending on the particular manufacturer who marketed them?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on what all kokade they would base their design on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember my wearing a kokade when I came to see the combatants at the front?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: On my chest?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also wore one very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you ever see me with a skull and bones kokade?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that, although I did have one like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not that I'm ashamed of that Chetnik tradition. The skull and bones was on the Chetnik kokade during the guerilla fighting against the Turks in Macedonia, was it not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm not that conversant with history. That was one of the versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the position of the leadership of the Serbian Radical Party was that not being ashamed of its past, we still consider this skull and bones to be outdated, something which was not befitting and we avoided using it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are quite right. That was what I asked Mr. Milenko Petrovic when he was the president in Sid. Once at the annual reunion, assembly of the Serbian Radical Party in Sid, the section of the Serbian Chetnik party paid tribute to me or honoured me and the citation said For his contribution to the fight in the -- in all the Serbian lands, it was blue, and at a certain part of this citation you could see the skull and bones emblem and I asked Petric, seeing that this is a symbol that is being avoided, why is it on these certificates of honour given to me, and it was also awarded to some other combatants, other participants in the war. Other things were also given, for instance, paintings, works of arts, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, the leadership of the party avoided to do this, but if a member wore one, we did not apply any political sanctions, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. There were different kokades. I as a participant never really paid attention. I never said to anyone, Look, you are wearing Djujic's kokade, you are wearing Seselj's kokade, you are wearing Draskovic's kokade, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This was up to the free will, to the free choice of every soldier of every combatant, to wear what they pleased?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the units that I was part of, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the army officers sometimes tried to prevent that practice and -- but mainly did right, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tried, but if the overwhelming majority was against, they desisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So in order not to undermine the combat morale, they simply tolerated that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was there ever a mass production of traditional old Chetnik standards, flags, with this skull and bones or with such standards, such flags appeared, was this just a very unskilled manual product?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about mass production. I have one at home which I paid a lad to make for me. It had the skull and bones emblem and it was written with faith in God, freedom or death, Chetnik from Srem, and I often gave it to people, to wedding parties in my city and they would often carry it in front of the wedding party. It was used and that is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But these were all just single products. I mean, some people were more skilled and the others made them in a more primitive fashion, but you could hardly find two same ones?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These black Chetnik flags, yes, one could hardly find two same flags of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Sometimes they were used by the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party at their own initiative but also they were used by many other combatants, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you, say a man would have a wedding party the next day, he would be getting married, and he would have 200 guests and he would ask me to lend my flag to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I just wanted to clarify this. It's not something that it was the exclusive property of the Serb Radical Party and its section of the Serb Radical-- the Serb Chetnik Movement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether that was compulsory when you joined the section that you'd get a flag and things like that. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, when you became a member, you didn't get anything else except for a membership card of the Serb Radical Party, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Later on they also issued this little booklet saying the Serbian Chetnik Movement section.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But this was done by local functionaries at their own initiative?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There wasn't a central organisation of this kind?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You talked about fighting in Vukovar and about my visit. You described me touring the front line. You described that at one point in time I even shot at the enemy positions from the front line.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Prvomajska Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was shooting at this blue building where the members of the Croatian paramilitary forces were.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the other side, that was considered to be area that was not in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I seem to remember this blue building. Maybe it was a supermarket or something like that.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was this building that we used to call the mini market. So as far as I can remember, you were a bit further away from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was at the front line of the Croat positions, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Croat --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that it is impossible to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that I gave encouragement to the combatants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we're being asked by the interpreters for to you slow down. It's hard for them to keep up. Page 74, line 8. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I insist on maximum discipline of the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party and the other soldiers that I came across?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct-- or, rather, of course, you never encouraged a lack of discipline, that is not something characteristic of you. You were saying things like, Fight an honourable fight and bear in mind the legacy of honourable Serb soldiers, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now I'm going to try to interpret what it was that I was saying and then you are going to confirm to me whether that was the way it was or not, because I remember this better, and it also has to do with a great many times that I spoke. Did I say at the front line, Fight like heroes, but show chivalry, behaving humanely towards prisoners, civilians on the other side, women and children like the Serb Knights did through history? Was that roughly what I was saying?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of such speeches of yours. Now, literally whether it was in that order, well, I wouldn't mind saying that that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Witness, we're now addressing important issues about Vukovar. Do you confirm hearing from Mr. Seselj personally that prisoners, women, children, had to be protected? Did you hear him say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have just clarified that, that Mr. Seselj tried to remind me of the speeches that he was making at the time, and how it was that he was speaking. As I'm saying, it looks like that but I did not say yes precisely. That's what I remember. I remember that quotation, that sentence precisely in that way. At any rate, he came to give us encouragement. He did have a certain system in terms of how he did this. What Mr. Seselj said now, I really don't see why I wouldn't believe him, that that is exactly what he was saying, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But as far as you can remember, did he say that prisoners, women and children had to be protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've just said, Your Honour, that I do not know in which way he spoke, but at any rate I don't remember the speech in Vukovar that he was calling upon us to go and shoot someone, execute someone, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't therefore remember or say precisely that Mr. Seselj would have in his public speeches at the time, including in Vukovar, addressed the fact that prisoners, women and children had to be protected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did not attend the public gathering in Vukovar. All of this, I mean we heard Mr. Seselj and perhaps someone else too. As he walked, as he toured the front line this was very short. Whether he made a speech afterwards in Vukovar, I don't know, but that is not literally the speech. Quite simply, he would be talking to a group of people around him in a very loud manner characteristic of him and then he was saying these things, and now he explained this one sentence that he stated, but I cannot say yes, that is exactly what you said. But I know that I do not remember that then at that time when he visited Vukovar that he said, Go out and if you have some prisoners, go out and execute them. No, he didn't say that, either. I hope that you understand this now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I tried to do now, to quote myself, I cannot give a verbatim quote after so many years, either. Did this correspond to the essence of all the things I said before the combatants? There was no speech in Vukovar but did I talk to people, isn't that right, as I toured the front lines?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Surrounded by commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Does what I said to you now correspond to the essence of what I was saying there? I'm not asking for you verbatim confirmation of every one of my statements. I cannot do that myself, let alone you. Was this the essence of what I was saying, that the prisoners should not be mistreated and...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The witness has been asked and answered the question several times that he doesn't recall Mr. Seselj saying this. I think that this is repetitive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You said that you did not remember. But Mr. Seselj is dealing with the essence of what he might have said. So what can you say about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was my understanding of Mr. Seselj's visit to Vukovar that time that he came to boost our morale and it was not my understanding that he was trying to talk us into doing something evil. I never heard you say something like that ever, go out and kill whoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned that when I was touring the front line that we came across seven dead Croatian paramilitaries, seven, four plus three policemen, that is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure now, but we had liquidated them the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In combat?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were not caught and executed. They were killed in combat. It's important for me to have that established here. I mentioned that these corpses should be burned. Do you remember that I said burned or did I say buried?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that you used that word in order to prevent a disease from breaking out, that they should be gotten rid of, burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As an experienced soldier, Mr. Stoparic, you should understand that if somebody had burned seven or nine corpses there that all of Vukovar would have smelled?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I'm not that stupid not to know the burning of seven or nine corpses causes disastrous problems for the people who are there.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, well, I don't even know why it was that I remember that. Probably I was listening and I needed to hear you, actually you -- I thought that you would really praise us for this kind of action, but after that, I realised that we didn't do everything right. Now, why this is in my thoughts, the word "burned," I really don't want to accuse anyone, believe me. I just seem to remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What I remember is that I said that the corpses should be buried as soon as possible in order to prevent a disease from breaking out.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that I wasn't the one who made a mistake or perhaps later on when recounting this, somebody had perhaps added a sentence of their own, that's the assumption, but I really had no intention of including something that you had not said. After all, it is 1991 and one has to remember all of that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, the point was to prevent the outbreak of a disease.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only of a disease, but also the cattle would start eating corpses if they were there for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Pigs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dogs?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned -- I'm going to put one more question to you and probably it is time to take the break, and then after the break we're going to move on to the situation regarding Ovcar. You mentioned that when a year after the liberation of Vukovar, there was a celebration, it was in the centre of town, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was there too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After this celebration, we went to Stanko Vujanovic's cafe, we were invited there, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I sat there, too. No, not quite literally close to you but a few tables away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I was there and then my associates from the leadership of the party and then Captain Radic -- Major Radic afterwards.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember Radic exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were some other officers and I remember him, too.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, both people are speaking at the same time now. Interpreter's note that a considerable portion is missing now.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard about this from him, that you promised to have a drunk when we win. Otherwise, you don't drink; I know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Can we ask Mr. Seselj to go back a couple of questions, because the interpreters indicated that they were unable to follow the speaker, and the overlap has prevented an accurate record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that, Mr. President, this is not being taken from my time, because what I'm worried about the most is the amount of time that I will have available. I want to have all details clarified during the cross-examination of this witness. But briefly I'm going to repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When the first anniversary of the liberation of Vukovar was being commemorated, I come to a celebration in the centre of town. After that, we were invited to the cafe owned by Stanko Vujanovic. Then we sat there, we talked, we had a few drinks, most of them soft drinks, perhaps somebody drank alcohol, too, and then we went our separate ways. That's the essence. Is that right? I interpret this right, your words?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that is the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When I was in Vukovar, while I was touring the front line, did you walk all the time along with these people who were going with me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last thing I saw was when you wanted to shoot and when little Dzo - do you remember little Dzo - Dzo Valjarevic [phoen], do you remember his nickname, whatever his real name was? He stood in front of you and you said to him, No, you are so small that you cannot protect me if anything should happen and them probably Kameni send him -- rather, went to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Little Dzo at the front line stood in front of me in order to protect me from enemy fire, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And I made a bit of a joke, saying that you are so small that you cannot protect me, something like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, there is another thing that is important for me. Since you were over there among the escorts at the front line, did you ever hear me during the fighting for Vukovar during that visit, that I had a meeting with the officers in Stanko Vujanovic's house? Have you ever heard of anything like that? I really don't know how long you stayed in Vukovar at all and where you went.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spent a night there, somewhere near the front line. I'm going to remind you that during the night by that house, the agricultural air force of the Croatian side threw a heater full of explosive. We thought that that was because of your visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But it was said that that is why it was done, because I was there, and Milorad Albijanic [phoen], an official from some Serb association from Kosovo slept there with me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Later on there was a joke that I just turned to the other side and went on sleeping and he got up and could not sleep any longer, so we laughed about that the next day. And then there is this photograph as well of the well-known Serb photographer as I'm washing my face naked to the waist in front of that house on the following morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's time for the break. Mr. Seselj, you will resume after the break with the problem of the photograph. It's 20 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can your -- can your staff have these documents distributed? I have copies for the members of the Trial Chamber and a copy for the Prosecutor and a copy for the witness. I gave these documents on the 3rd of January to have them translated, but the Mr. Doraiswamy told me that it can only be translated by the end of January, and I need to use this during the cross-examination of this witness, so could he please be given a copy so that he could prepare for that, too, and could the Prosecutor and the members of the Trial Chamber be given copies as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document is being handed around and we will resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Seselj, just before the break, you handed us eight documents and told us that these eight documents couldn't be translated by the translation department, the CLSS. I understand that the CLSS was unable to translate this. But when this happens, before the hearing, you can give these documents to the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution, even in B/C/S, so that the Prosecution can get ready for it, and the Prosecution -- in the Prosecutor's office, you know, there are people who speak B/C/S and who can know exactly what the document is about and then they can get prepared. That way you're sure that the Prosecution will not raise an objection regarding this -- any document. Of course, I'm not blaming you. You asked for the CLSS to translate this early in January and they were not able to do that. We'll try to make do. Just tell the witness, Take this document. In such-and-such paragraph, you can find this or that. What do you think of it. And then we will see what the scope of the document is. Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I object to Mr. Seselj using these documents without providing a copy that is in one of the working languages of the Tribunal. I can't read them, and therefore, he can't use them. Sorry. We've had sufficient recesses during January that he could have pointed out these exact ones to put priority on them or even announce the problem at the beginning of today's session to have rough translations made. And I don't think it is appropriate to shift the translation burden to OTP staff.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I be allowed to say something on the subject? Judges, I think that the same yard-stick should be applied to me and to the representative of the indictment, to the Prosecution, and towards me, that yard-stick should be even boarder, because in these proceedings I must be privileged, as the accused, compared to the Prosecution with all its apparatus standing behind it. And I would like to remind you that when we had Oberschall, the expert witness, that the Prosecution, the day before the hearing, provided a document about his interview and testimony without even providing me with the additional documents in English to this day, the part that I -- that I launched a protest for them being in English, and I said why were they in English so I don't use them. Secondly, I don't have to base my examination on these documents at all, but you must apply the same criterion to me and to the Prosecution. That is the bare minimum of a requirement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber believes that the criterion should be the same on both parties. Now, without putting the blame on anyone, on January 3rd you sent these documents to the translation department. That was 20 days ago, and this document has not been translated, even though 20 days have elapsed. It's not your fault. Secondly, Prosecution is telling us that it raises an objection because it did not obtain the document in one of the Tribunal's working languages. You're absolutely correct in saying so, Ms. Dahl. But the translation department belongs to the Registrar. The Registrar is a body in this Tribunal. So is the -- the OTP, so are the Judges. Obviously the Tribunal is not functioning correctly. It's not up to the accused to be subjected to this failure. So we need to kind some kind of practical solution, and the practical solution is that in the future, Mr. Seselj, if he has documents in Serbian which were not translated, he will hand them over to you as quickly as possible, and it will be up to you to find a solution. As a professional, even if you don't know anything about the document, just like I do, wait for the questions, wait for the answer of the witness, and then we can see, on a case by case basis, what is the context of this document. We don't know yet what the question is going to be. We have no idea what topic the accused is going to deal with; but as a professional, I can face any situation. I'm not going to be put off balance just because suddenly I'm handed a document in a language that I cannot read. I know the question will be translated, I know the answers -- the witness is going to answer, and since the cross-examination will continue tomorrow, you and everyone helping you will have the possibility of translating the document overnight, and you can ask additional questions during the re-direct. It is true that we're working in two official languages, but there are some situations where, of course, you're not to blame, I'm not to blame, but unfortunately, the translation department was not able to do the job. We're not going to stop the trial, saying let's wait for these documents to be translated and have questions about these documents. I don't see what you could say as an answer, but you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My suggestion is that we have the translations completed overnight, perhaps. We have not heard what the delay is or what the anticipated time to translate them is, or we can also go into private session. Because I think it's unsafe to proceed where I am unable to anticipate problems based on a review of the document and I consider, with respect, that we serve different roles and that the willingness of the Bench to proceed with a document it can't read is distinctly different than disadvantaging the Prosecution's ability to articulate proper objections and protect sensitive information and avoid error.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, these eight documents, are these statements, testimonies? It seems that it is the case so that these documents have been certified and authenticated. Could you tell us what these documents about? Are there mention of protected witnesses in them? I know nothing about these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Judge. First of all, I'm categorically opposed to the request made by the Prosecution, and then I'd like to remind you, once again, that in the cross-examination of expert witness Oberschall, well, I conducted the cross-examination without having received a proposal of the very important documents to this day which the Prosecution brought forth at the very last moment during the proceedings. Secondly, here we're talking about statements by a bus driver; his name is Nikola Tumic; Drago Mrdja, Savan Vidovic, Zoran Medic, Mrko Tutsakovic, Semo Cojdar, Bogdan Petrovic, Vaso Djurdjovic. That is to say, statements which were given before a court in Serbia and have been authenticated, and from it, we can see that these were bus drivers and, as such, they sent back all of the volunteers, took back of the volunteers, the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, from Vukovar to Serbia immediately after Vukovar's liberation, and Vukovar was liberated on the 18th of November. And they transported the volunteers on the 18th, 19th, and 20th of November, taking them to Serbia. And Ovcara took place in the night between 20th and 21st of November. So I wanted to use this document -- these documents in the cross-examination of this witness. If you're not going to allow me to do so, I won't insist. I will throw them away. I'm just asking to be treated equally with -- as -- an equal attitude towards me and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right in telling us about the Oberschall precedent, and you're telling us these are bus drivers. We're going to relate how they drove the volunteers back. I have a excellent memory, and I do remember that at one point in time you told us that, regarding Vukovar, the volunteers came back before the events that occurred during the night from the 20th to the 21st, and these documents obviously -- or seem to prove that your volunteers had left the premises before crimes were committed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the night between the 20th and 21st, the crime took place at Ovcara, the execution of 200 Croatian prisoners, and the volunteers were on their way back on the 18th, 19th, and 20th, just to be precise on that score.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is absolutely what I said. I said that, according to you, these documents would prove that the volunteers had left the premises before the crimes were committed. That's what I said. Maybe there was a translation error. So, please, ask your questions, starting from this and we'll play it by ear. At this point in time, I have no reason to believe that these documents are authentical, and then according to the content, with the questions and the answers of the witnesses, we will see. The witness was there, he was on the premises, and he can confirm whether these documents seem to be telling the truth or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I have a number of questions to ask and we'll get to that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, indirectly you told me that you had never heard of a meeting of mine with the officers of the Guards Brigade in Stanko Vujanovic's house when I visited Vukovar during the war. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You heard of a meeting like that? But you do remember meeting in Stanko Vujanovic's cafe one year after the liberation of Vukovar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps you don't understand the gist of my question. I'm asking you so that you could give me an answer because there's a false witness who has moved this meeting a year forward in Stanko Vujanovic's cafe. That's why I needed your answer, just to let you know why I'm insisting on this. You know Milan Lancuzanin, Kameni, the commander of the Leva Supoderica Detachment, you know him well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that, well yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was he a strict commander?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What about towards others, I assume that he was strict towards them too?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about myself as a commander of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Did he prohibit any type of mistreatment of prisoner of war their execution the maltreatment of women, children, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never ordered any mistreatment and if he would learn about something, and the example of this unfortunate Topola.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Expelled him from the detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could he have done anything else but to send him away?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he couldn't have shot him. All he do have done was send him away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And Topola was suspected of having killed a young girl. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You tried to investigate that but did not succeed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well there was intensive action going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You mean the intensity of the fighting to investigate fully?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right it was forgotten. The man was forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But anyway he was sent away. He stayed in Vukovar. But he wasn't in Leva Supoderica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down, please, for the benefit of one and all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, you're speaking much too fast. As Judge Harhoff told you, advised you, count to five before you start answering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And can I add, that these proceedings will not make any meaning unless the Bench is able to understand what is being said. So in your own interests, try and keep it slow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Yes, I will do my best, and I'll wait to see the translation come up on the screen. My adrenaline is up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for answering you said something that almost -- that surprises me and I would like to look into this. Regarding Topola and Kameni, you're saying -- you say they couldn't do anything. So in military terms I'm quite surprised. If a serviceman commits any kind of thing, you know there are procedures. There can be an investigation, there's a military prosecutor, investigative judge. I even think that in wartime, I haven't looked into the military code of the former Yugoslavia, but I think that you could have martial courts, you know, that are convened immediately and that try the accused immediately and if there is a capital punishment, the accused can be executed if found guilty. So when you say that Kameni and Topola could do nothing, could you please give me an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honour, to paint the picture. Kameni, as the commander, or he was komandir. And myself as the platoon commander. He appointed me as platoon commander and at that time I wasn't even a reserve officer. He was a reserve officer and he had some knowledge; and I should have had because I did my regular military service. But what I want to say is this, the point of what I'm saying is this, we as officers, we're not professional officers of the Yugoslav People's Army most probably a professional soldier or an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army would now how to behave and what to do but quite simply the situation was such that there was many actions going on and perhaps Kameni did send up this information to his superiors. I don't know about that, but I said that he could not do anything. There was nothing he could do. He couldn't take over the power in his own hands and that he penalise, be the judge and jury in this case and punish someone. So the best thing he could do was to exclude him from the unit, to send him away. There was no other practice open to us that we knew about. We weren't trained as active duty officers ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well thank you for your answer. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, do you happen to know that during all these wars that there was ever a court martial sitting and that anybody was executed for any crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anything like that happen on the Croatian or the Muslim side have you ever heard of anything like that happen?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that anything like that ever happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So we agree that in this war, court martials did not operate anywhere and nobody was executed for any crimes or offences. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I know of no example on any side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now we can lament over the fact that that was not the case. But that's how things stood. Very well, Mr. Stoparic. Now let's go back to the question of Ovcara. You know that when Vukovar was liberated on the 18th of November, that the JNA immediately endeavoured to reduce the number of men in the area because much of the man power was hampering normalisation of life in the area?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They tried to establish civil control or civilian control in town and immediately after the fall of Vukovar the Guards Brigade was withdrawing from the territory and another brigade coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. And they started transporting the volunteers back to Serbia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes they did start that in Leva Supoderica over several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In three days.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was disbanded many stayed on but during that week many left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But in the space of three days the bulk left for Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the bulk did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There were those who wanted to stay on and live in Vukovar. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I myself remained for a time precisely because I didn't need organised transport because I lived 30 kilometres away from my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But that's why they didn't manage to write down your participation war in the Guards Brigade because the Guards Brigade withdrew, so you had to go to Belgrade to command there. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did get some certificate a certificate of some kind in Velepromet proving that I was member of Leva Supoderica, but I gave that to a corporal in the guards brigade who paid out my salary during my stay in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned little Dzo, Mali Dzo who was a volunteer. Do you remember that he stayed on to live in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived in Vukovar for a years. I think Solobodan Katic too?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Katic lived in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He got married?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slobodan Katic was in the Territorial Defence of Vukovar, something like that. And Mali Dzo -- little Dzo opened a book shop, did he not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes I will slow down. I will slow down but my promises might seem to be a little funny when I forget to keep my promises during the heat of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I for example remember that at the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party, we presented little Dzo with many of my books to sell in his own book store and that he could finance his livelihood. We didn't ask him to give us any money from the sale of those books. I remember that detail. Slobodan Katic stayed on to; you confirmed that yourself. And his function in the Territorial Defence? Well, he requested Ljubisa Petkovic to put forward the promotion of certain officers; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we saw a document to that effect, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes we did. We saw a paper to that effect. Now Ljubisa Petkovic, to whom could he have made that proposal except to the corresponding service in the General Staff? Was there anyone else he could make those proposals to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that's what I said, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine. So it was common knowledge that Ljubisa Petkovic, representing the Serb Radical Party, was in charge of contacts with the General Staff, liaising with the General Staff, and that he had firm cooperation with the head of the personnel department or the department for mobilisation, whatever it was called. But everybody knew about that; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That he could make proposals like that? All right, fine. Now, you have described here the behaviour and conduct of Kameni when the crime of Ovcara took place. You were an eye-witness, were you not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that a crime had been committed. I didn't know at the time. All I knew was that something was going on .

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Kameni was very excited, he was angry, he was nervous, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could describe it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And by his demeanour he showed that something terrible had happened, which should not have happened in any -- under any circumstances?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. I socialised with Kameni after the war a lot, almost on a daily basis, so it is difficult for me to testify at times because I don't want to say something that he told me about later on. But even what he told me later on coincides with what I saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now did Kameni always condemn the crime?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he always said that it was quite ludicrous.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That it should never have happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that kind of meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now do you link Kameni with the crime? Do you think that Kameni could have taken part in that crime since you knew him very well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said many times and I think I repeated it here in court that it is my personal conviction that he was not involved, and I even try to speak about judgment from Serbia where it says that he didn't kill anybody there or whatever it says in the judgment. I just read about it in the papers, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how much did you know at that time about the situation in Serbia? Was it quite clear to at that time that the special regime court in Belgrade had actually convicted the innocent Kameni to -- sentence him to 20 years of imprisonment only in order to create an artificial link between me myself as his friend and Ovcara. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm almost certain and I'm almost convinced that he is innocent and as to the wanting to establish a link, I cannot say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you wear two hats. You're an accused but, at the same time you're also representing yourself as a lawyer. And now I'm addressing the lawyer in you. You mentioned this judgment convicting Kameni. I have this question. In Serbia, judgments in criminal cases, do they have to be reasoned or is there absolutely no grounds given, because if he was convicted to 20 years, I suppose that that had to be reasoned. One has to account for this conviction. So my question is a simple one. This judgment, in theory you must have it, is it a reasoned one or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, that judgment was reasoned in language that was not quite coherent, but the most important thing is that it was overturned by the supreme Court both in relation to the part which refers to Kameni and that the entire -- that there was a new trial. This new trial is still going on. So this orchestrated judgment was overturned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, so you're telling us that the Supreme Court ordered a new trial which would explain why there is currently a trial going on. So legally speaking, we do not know whether Mr. Kameni is guilty or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Legally speaking we don't know. But here the witness is not speaking as a jurist. The witness here appears as an eye-witness to certain events, and he is actually relating his own experience in that connection and the information that he has in that connection. Of course, I have the right to put him some questions that are a bit more leading in the cross-examination stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, did the Leva Supoderica Detachment have any connection with Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Velepromet several times to replenish our food supplies and for such things there was always the military police there and some representatives of the civilian authorities. But I don't know of any links of the kind that you ask about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So Velepromet was a depot, a warehouse, a place where prisoners of war would be detained before being dispatched to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Is that right? Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where the civilian authorities of Slavonia Branja Western Srem et cetera? You never even posted guards there from your detachment, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we were combatants we were combatants, we were sentinels at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you confirm my statement that there was no connection between you and Velepromet except that you went there to get your supplies and necessities for daily life?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And if you did take a Croatian soldier prisoner you would then assign him to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To the military and the army would take them where it was -- he was to be taken?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you never kept a soldier yourself prisoner?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As I understood your statement Topola actually snatched a prisoner from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said in the examination-in-chief that in a way he stole this prisoner, snatched him as it were, from the place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So this has nothing to do with your detachment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he snatched this prisoner -- I apologise, I don't know precisely or exactly, but I think it was on saint -- on the archangel's day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is the 21st of November. That is the day of the liberation of Vukovar? That is after Ovcara, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a member -- a member after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That is several days after the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that Saint Archangel Michael is celebrated on the 21st of November?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not my patron saint, but this person actually snatched a prisoner and took him as a gift to the person whose patron saint of -- he was celebrating.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unable to follow the parties...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour. I would like this to be more than a private conversation between the witness and the accused. I really need them to allow for interpretation, otherwise, as the Judge Harhoff mentioned before, it excludes the Bench from receiving the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we were -- you were very fast here in dealing with this topic, which is an important one. This Topola, Witness, it seems to appear, from listening to questions and answers, that he stole something from a detainee in Velepromet. But the theft and the date of the theft seems to coincide with the Saint Michael's day, the archangel's day, which is later than the 21st. Therefore, when Topola did this theft, he no longer belonged to the Leva Supoderica Detachment. Apparently most of the members of the detachment had left in buses, and he stayed with a legal status that we shall determine later on, but on that day, he was no longer a member of the unit you were in charge of. Is that how we should understand things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several days before the official fall or liberation of Vukovar, he was removed by the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And why was he removed? Not because of the theft in Velepromet, because that occurred later, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was removed because the -- he was suspected of having raped a girl, a women, and having thrown her into a well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the reason why he had been removed. And if we understand Mr. Seselj's questions properly, the theft in Velepromet occurred after the date of the 21st. Anyway, after he had been removed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I think that is a little clear now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it is my fault, Judge, for speaking too fast. He snatched a Croatian prisoner. He unlawfully took him out of the Velepromet warehouse intending to kill him. That is the sense of Mr. Stoparic's statement in the examination in chief. It was not a theft of property. He unlawfully took out a prisoner. It was a figure of speech. He took him out unlawfully and that took place several days after the fall of Vukovar. That is what is of the essence for us right now. So not even that event can be associated with the Leva Supoderica Detachment, right.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only link is that he went into the house of this person who was celebrating and that he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the only link is that the Chinese who was -- that Kinez who was in your staff actually saved this prisoner?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He informed us of what was happening but nobody dared actually speak back, talk back, contradict Topola.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is very sorry but the interpreter did not actually hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, did look at these statements which I gave you during the break?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked to but I was not allowed to take them out of the courtroom. I did take a look while I was waiting for the Bench to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You see that this -- these are statements of bus drivers who were taking volunteers back to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you notice here that the driver explicitly say that the bulk of the volunteers were from the Serbian Radical Party; that they were disciplined, that none of them had weapons; that they were escorted at all times by the military police; that they were searched on entering Serbia; that even official dogs would be used for searches.
