That is to say trained dogs who could detect weapons by smell, the smell of the grease used to lubricate the weapons or the smell of black powder and similar. Did you see that here?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the first two statements completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They are similar more or less. You could give your comment on the basis of these first two statements. Do you think that they are truthful?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How the volunteers fared when they were going home from Vukovar is something that I don't know, but it is certainly my experience when I was passing through Serbia on a bus as a volunteer that there were always strict controls including of weaponry both when we were going into the terrain and vice versa it would be carried out, I mean these checks by either the civilian or the military police, and this is also indicated by the driver. And what the driver says is most probably true, that this is the way they were taken back to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not a single volunteer was drunk, according to these statements right? Also during the searches there was no -- there were no grounds to detain or arrest any of them or similar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They probably had nothing on there which was prohibited. They were not drunk or I'm not sure. Maybe they may have been celebrating because of the fall of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They also say, some of the drives that they have no technical goods with them. Was there any control to establish whether anyone of them had stolen any washing machines or cooking ranges or TV sets.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After the fall -- or liberation of Vukovar, was it strict -- was it strict in connection with the liberation of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this border crossing point where they were crossing there was control and check carried out but near Sid there at the border it was more relaxed. Later it grew into a more strict border crossing point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could anyone take out any stolen goods?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this crossing yes, but not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know of any instances of Serbian Radical Party members exporting anything stolen from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, had I seen that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, had you seen that or do you know for sure that they did something.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an organised fashion --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, because something of value has to be organised. If is it of no value can you put it your pocket, but we're talking about some more -- some technical equipment that is worth more, then it had to be organised?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you didn't see that. Well, Mr. Stoparic, upon returning to Vukovar, according to your statement, in the beginning of year 2000 joined the Serbian Radical Party, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what the date was when I became a member of the Serbian Radical Party, but I know that that took place at Milenko Petrovic's house, which does not mean that there was an office already in place, but this is where I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We do not need the exact date. Was it in the beginning of 1992?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I may have been joined even in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. It may have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes it could have been that, because Kameni also joined in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe, I'm not quite sure where I joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did anyone prescribe the obligation for all members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment to have to join the Serb Radical Party was that compulsory?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we the commanders, the komandiri, we all did that as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But was anyone forcing you, did anyone coerce you do to that or did you do that on a voluntary basis because you wanted to?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wanted to. I explicitly wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the next time you went to the front as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party, right. That -- we're now already talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go. I don't know to which terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I shall remind you that was the unit which was led by Branislav Vakic in Herzegovina. Did you not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or perhaps before that, perhaps I was before that in -- I took a flight from Belgrade to Bihac and then from Bihac we went -- I went to Bosansko Grahovo and that terrain, and that is quite possible that that took place before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could have you gone to Bosanski Grahovo as a member -- as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party or a member of some other formation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bubanj Potok to the airport and then to Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But not as a member of the Serb Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With a mediation of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, you're going too fast. Before going go back to that question I realised that Mr. Seselj asked a question and you didn't quite answer it and it may be a relevant question. He asked you whether all volunteers who were members of the Leva Supoderica Detachment were members of the Serbian Radical Party. You answered at line 6, page 102, Yes, the commanders. But I would like to know - and I think that was the meaning of the question - did all the members or were all the members of that unit members of the Serbian Radical Party, or were there some like you or others but not all of them, as far as you know. Were there members in that unit who were not members of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not all of them were members of the Serb Radical Party. Many perhaps belonged to other parties. But most of them did not belong to a single party, quite simply people who considered themselves to be patriots and wanted to go into the war availed themselves of the opportunity provided by the Serb Radical Party to be sent to the front line. Now whether they joined up later, I don't know. So members of Leva Supoderica did not necessarily have to be members of the Radical Party and we did not put questions like that, who was a member of whose party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You answered in part, saying that there were in that unit members who belonged to other political parties. However, were there in that unit soldiers who did not belong to any political party, none at all? But as they were patriots they had decided to join that unit? Because you can be a patriot without being a member of a party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us any names of soldiers in that unit who were not members of any party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. An exceptionally good and brave man from Novi Sad, a squad leader, his name was Sasa. He was not a member of any party and I don't believe he is to this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I should move on to the question of Herzegovina because I assume that we don't have much time left for today so I would like to move on to that tomorrow. Judge, would you please be so kind as to tell me how much time we have?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see the clock. Ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Stoparic, you know that the Serb literary language consists of two dialects: The Ekavian and Ikavian?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were born in the Ekavian area. You always spoke Ekavian, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the area I was born in and that's how I speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you do understand Ikavian?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there's also some new self-styled Croatian words that were artificially inserted in the language and that neither you nor I understand, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes when I watch Croatian television it does happen that I don't understand something, but in the context of a sentence I tend to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what the word Postrojba means?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know what Satnija means?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Regiment? No, Mr. Stoparic, it means company.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it's a military term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Seselj, because the words in your language are not in the transcript. It might be important for them to be. Then have you got to spell the words then it will be noted in the transcript, it will be recorded; otherwise you can see the sign showing that the word is not recorded and it's ignored. Of course, if you think it is important, if you don't, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is very important, Judge. First of all, I asked Mr. Stoparic whether he knew what the word Postrojba means; he did know although this is a newly invented Croatian expression. He said that it meant unit. And then I asked him whether he know what Satnija means. S-a-t-n-i-j-a. He didn't know. His answer was that it meant regiment and I said to him that it meant company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now what is the rank of Satznik? It must be captain, right?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well, if Satnija is company then it has to be up to major at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It cannot be anything else -- captain. Mr. Stoparic, you do not use these terms Tocno, Promoviranje, Pozornost. Do you know what these words mean, the word Pozornost?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To look carefully, to observe carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To be careful, to pay attention but you don't understand -- but you don't that expression?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, when the Prosecutor was preparing you for this evidence, they were proofing you for days, four hours a day for several days. They gave you a statement to sign where, if they gave you a statement that included Satnija, Pozornost, Kolovoz, Ozujak, would you have corrected that straight away, would you have said immediately that could not have been your statement because you never spoke that way?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I speak the Serbian language. I can understand Kolovoz as asphalt or road but I don't speak that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Kolovoz means August in this sense, the month of August.

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also means road.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. So you would warn the Prosecution to the effect that these are not your words and that they could not be included in your statement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't talk that way so how can that be my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You would have said straight away, Ms. Dahl, I don't talk that way and it cannot be in my statement. Is that what you would have said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN STOPARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably that is what I would have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, what I have here is your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Mr. Seselj is now addressing an important issue which is the technique used in examination. If I understood properly, the accused noted in your statement, signed in your own language, that there were words that you would not use and you named quite a few of them. These words can be found, however, in your witness statement, in your language, which is B/C/S. So based on that, if what has been said is right, I have a question as to the way your statement was drafted. The investigators, when they were listening to you, did they first listen and then drafted the written statement but by putting into it words that you would not use, such as -- or words that a Croat would use. Is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigators have interpreters along with them. They put questions, I answer, and then these interpreters interpret at that same moment into English and into what you call B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've got the names of these interpreters. They are here in the paper. Were they interpreters who would tend to use - how shall I put it? - B/C/S or Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I intervene, Judge? I think it is important. I quoted the following terms or, rather, from the internal memorandum, it says the 10th of December, 2003. It should say the 10th of December, 2003, rather than Prosinac. It is sent by Gary Saxton and Dolijan Barag [phoen] and it says: Additions to the statement of Goran Stoparic. And then there is sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, these are paragraphs of his statement. Do you have that document? It is marked. Now will I manage to read this: 03456748, 03456751. I just have that designation. It's a total of six pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may. I have an internal memorandum dated 10 December 2003 from Gary Saxton and Dolijan Barag. It is not a statement signed by Mr. Stoparic but an internal memorandum recording an interview and notes. I -- it's in e-court as 65 ter Exhibit number 7035 and can I give you the English version. I believe it was translated at some point for disclosure purposes. It is not something that the witness reviewed and signed for correction of dialectal differences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed this internal memorandum is not signed so the witness is not aware of it. Mr. Seselj, if you refer to this internal memorandum, the witness is not involved because this memorandum only deals with the OTP. That records what the witness may have said, so I'm returning this document to the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I am aware of the fact that the witness did not directly participate in writing any one of these statements that is being ascribed to him. You can see that from the differences between his oral testimony and what is written in the statements. However, in these addenda the direct speech is used and the witness allegedly says: I was not involved in politics before the war; I was neither a Chetnik nor a communist. I don't know exactly when the office was opened. In the beginning of the war there weren't any Vojvodas, and so on and so forth. So these are direct quotations of his words that cannot correspond to the original. That is why I intervened. As for him not taking part in any one of the statements, we've already seen that here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think that Mr. Seselj is labouring under a misunderstanding. The process that produces a memorandum like this is a recollection of statements made by a witness written by -- into English originally by the investigator who's interviewed the witness to record the recollection of the interview. It is then translated into a language the accused understands for disclosure purposes. It does not purport to be a verbatim description in the original language of the witness. The investigators, of course, endeavour to capture as accurately as possible what the witness has said but the reason that we go to the formality that we have, for instance, in the statement signed and initialed on every page by the witness in 2006, is to try to capture the original words and language used by the witness. That's not what this document purports to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Dahl. Yes, Mr. Seselj, we want to avoid any misunderstanding for you or all other people. In fact, there are two categories of documents. The first category is his witness statement written in his language, translated into English and he signed each and every page of it. In other words, in theory, his written statement has been read again by him before he signed it and he read it again in his language so that the contents of it is supposed to be known to him, which would mean that if, in this written statement translated into his language, there are words that are more B/C/S than Serb words, that can come from the translation and the witness may not have noticed it. That's the first category of documents. The second one is the document mentioned just now by Ms. Dahl following the interview with the OTP. There was a internal memorandum drafted in English, then translated into B/C/S and disclosed to the Defence. So I think that's how things are to be understood.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, by your leave, may I say that the witness told you a few moments ago that these interviews were so exhausting that at the end he could hardly wait to sign all of that, so that it would be all over and done with. That is the essence of my intervention, that the witness actually was not even interested in checking whether everything in the statement corresponded to the essence of his words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be my last question and then we will end this hearing. Witness, you heard everything that was said. When you signed this written statement in your own language, did you take the time to read the entire document or did you just sign because you were told, Sign here and it's accurate? Could you tell us exactly how it happened, how you signed the document written in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, either somebody would read it out to me or I would read it myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you don't remember? You don't remember whether it was read out to you or whether you read it to yourself? You cannot be accurate about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When something is read out in the English language, the interpreter would read it out. When it was in my language, then I would read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, may I notice something. You see that what happens is that the witness even signs statements in English, that the interpreter interprets for him right there on the spot, and the witness does not have any proof of the text being exactly what the interpreter is telling him by way of an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I was wondering whether the presiding Judge's question related to the 2006 statement or some particular statement because Mr. Stoparic is now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2006. Very well, it is five after 7.00. The interpreters are going to be upset if we continue, so we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. See you tomorrow at 2.15 and we will continue this cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of January, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
